Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I leant upon a coppice gate When Frost was spectre-grey, And Winter's dregs made desolate The weakening eye of day. The tangled bine-stems scored the sky Like strings of broken lyres, And all mankind that haunted nigh Had sought their household fires. The land's sharp features seemed to be The Century's corpse outleant, His crypt the cloudy canopy, The wind his death-lament. The ancient pulse of germ and birth Was shrunken hard and dry, And every spirit upon earth Seemed fervourless as I. At once a voice arose among The bleak twigs overhead In a full-hearted evensong Of joy illimited; An aged thrush, frail, gaunt, and small, In blast-beruffled plume, Had chosen thus to fling his soul Upon the growing gloom. So little cause for carolings Of such ecstatic sound Was written on terrestrial things Afar or nigh around, That I could think there trembled through His happy good-night air Some blessed Hope, whereof he knew And I was unaware.

Resting against a wooden gate at the edge of a small wood, I observed the ghostly pale frost coating the scene while the dimming winter sun brought a desolate end to the day. High above, intertwining dry vines crisscrossed the sky like the snapped strings of a musical instrument, and all the local inhabitants had already retreated indoors to gather around their warm fireplaces. 

The stark lines of the frozen landscape resembled the lifeless body of the dying century, lying stretched out beneath a ceiling of heavy clouds, with the blowing wind sounding like a mournful funeral chant. The Earth's ancient rhythm of growth and renewal had withered into something dry and hard, and every living soul on the planet seemed just as devoid of energy and passion as I was.

Suddenly, a melody erupted from the barren branches overhead—a vibrant evening song overflowing with boundless joy. The singer was an elderly, frail, and tiny thrush with wind-blown feathers, who had chosen to pour his entire spirit into the deepening darkness. Because absolutely nothing in the surrounding world, near or far, offered any visible reason for such an ecstatic celebration, I was led to believe that his cheerful nighttime song held some sacred sense of optimism—a divine hope that the bird was aware of, but which remained completely hidden from me.

As the final embers of daylight fade into twilight, a profound solitude settles over a frozen, desolate landscape. The speaker stands entirely alone in the biting winter cold, an isolated witness to the dying day. While the rest of humanity has retreated indoors, seeking refuge and warmth beside their hearths, the speaker remains outdoors, exposed to the harsh elements and separated from the comfort of human companionship. 

This bleak and unforgiving environment is far more than a mere backdrop; it serves as a powerful symbol for the death of the nineteenth century itself. The tangled, leafless branches resemble the broken strings of a lyre, and the frozen earth appears as a vast tomb for the passing era. A pervasive sense of mortality hangs in the air, reflecting a total absence of vitality, warmth, and creative energy in the modern world. Life seems to have shrunk to a spiritless, moribund state, leaving the speaker suspended in a realm of absolute gloom and existential emptiness.

Yet, into this overwhelming darkness breaks an astonishing sound. From the frost-bitten boughs, an aged and frail thrush unexpectedly erupts into song. The bird itself is a picture of vulnerability—gaunt, battered by the wind, and wearing plumage thinned by time. Despite its diminished physical state and the overwhelming misery of its surroundings, the thrush pours its entire soul into an ecstatic, full-hearted melody of unbridled joy.

Surveying the dreary surroundings, the speaker struggles to comprehend the catalyst for such passionate celebration. There is no visible reason in the frozen earth, the bleak sky, or the dying century to justify such an outpouring of happiness. From a rational, human perspective, the environment offers only reasons for despair, making the bird's triumphant carol seem entirely detached from physical reality.

Ultimately, this miraculous song forces a profound shift in the speaker's consciousness. Though the speaker remains unable to find any logical cause for optimism in the bleak landscape, the thrush’s unyielding joy suggests that a "Blessed Hope" exists—one that transcends the limits of human reason. The bird seems privy to a divine or cosmic truth that humanity, bogged down by intellect and sorrow, can no longer perceive. In the end, the thrush leaves the speaker with a quiet, enduring revelation: even in the darkest and most hopeless of times, a reason for joy persists beyond the boundary of human understanding.
outputs.L4:
I leant upon a coppice gate when Frost was spectre-grey, and Winter’s dregs made desolate the weakening eye of day. The landscape before me seemed to hold its breath, frozen in a state of suspended animation. Tangled plant stems reached toward the overcast sky like the broken strings of a long-abandoned lyre, useless and silent against the biting cold. It was more than merely the end of a winter afternoon; it felt like the final, exhausted gasps of an entire era. The century itself seemed to lie stretched out like a corpse, the cloudy canopy serving as its crypt, and the moaning wind its mournful funeral song. 

In this vast expanse of death and decay, every spirit upon the earth seemed as devoid of passion and vitality as my own. I stood alone in the creeping gloom, watching all other living creatures retreat to the warmth of their firesides. As I observed the barren trees and the hardened earth, I felt an overpowering sense of existential dread. My internal world mirrored the desolate horizon: I saw no promise in the future, no lingering warmth in the past, and no purpose in the present. The death of the century was the death of my own optimism, leaving behind a cold, hollow cynicism that felt impossible to shatter.

Then, without warning, the oppressive silence was broken. 

High among the bleak, frost-covered twigs, a sound erupted that seemed entirely alien to the dead world around us. It was a voice raised in unbounded joy, pouring out a full-hearted song into the gathering darkness. I looked up, expecting perhaps a grand or majestic creature, but found only an aged thrush. He was frail, gaunt, and small, his feathers ruffled raggedly by the icy wind. He had every reason to huddle in silence, to surrender to the cold just as the rest of the world had done. Instead, this decrepit little bird chose to fling his entire soul into the gloom, singing with an ecstatic, radiant fervour that defied the grim reality of his surroundings.

I listened in quiet astonishment. There was nothing in the frozen earth below, nor in the darkening skies above, to justify such a triumphant melody. There was no hint of spring, no sudden bloom, no warmth to account for his ecstasy. Yet, he sang on, his music cutting through the bleak air with incandescent joy. 

In that profound moment, I realized that the thrush possessed a secret to which I was entirely blind. Some "Blessed Hope"—a deep, transcendent truth woven into the fabric of creation—was known to him, though it remained hidden from my own despairing mind. I was still trapped in my gloomy isolation, burdened by the death of the century and my own hopelessness. Yet, through the thrush's ecstatic song, I was forced to acknowledge that even in the darkest, most desolate corners of existence, a divine and unknowable joy endures, vibrant and invincible, just beyond the reach of human reason.

**Frost** is nature’s most delicate ironwork. **When** dawn breaks, it reveals a landscape rimed in silver glass: every blade of grass stands as a tiny crystal blade, **and** every window pane bears the intricate, feathered geometry of the cold. The garden, once loud with the hum of bees **and** the rustle of green life, now sits suspended in a peaceful, motionless sleep.

There is a distinct clarity to this first turning of the season. **When** you step out onto the crunchy earth, your breath curls upward like mist, **and** the crisp air fills your lungs with a cold, clarifying shock. The warmth **and** chaos of summer are long gone, replaced by sharp shadows, pale light, **and** the quiet comfort of the earth settling down to rest.

counterfactuals.output:
Here is the complete text of **"The Darkling Thrush"** by Thomas Hardy (originally published in December 1900):

***

### The Darkling Thrush

**I**
I leant upon a coppice gate
    When Frost was spectre-grey,
And Winter's dregs made desolate
    The weakening eye of day.
The tangled bine-stems scored the sky
    Like strings of broken lyres,
And all mankind that haunted nigh
    Had sought their household fires.

**II**
The land's sharp features seemed to be
    The Century's corpse outleant,
His crypt the cloudy canopy,
    The wind his death-lament.
The ancient pulse of germ and birth
    Was shrunken hard and dry,
And every spirit upon earth
    Seemed fervourless as I.

**III**
At once a voice arose among
    The bleak twigs overhead
In a full-hearted evensong
    Of joy illimitable;
An aged thrush, frail, gaunt, and small,
    In blast-beruffled plume,
Had chosen thus to fling his soul
    Upon the growing gloom.

**IV**
So little cause for carolings
    Of such ecstatic sound
Was written on terrestrial things
    Afar or nigh around,
That I could think there trembled through
    His happy good-night air
Some blessed Hope, whereof he knew
    And I was unaware.

The crimson sun sinks low and slow
Behind the stark and frozen bough;
The twilight bleeds a muted glow
Upon the winter’s furrowed brow.

The century wanes, its glory spent,
Beneath a vault of leaden gray;
The monuments of man are bent,
And ancient grandeur fades away.

A silent gloom enfolds the plain,
The bitter winds forget to blow;
I stand amid the lingering pain
Of all that perished long ago.

The world grows old, its hearth fires die,
An epoch hushed in icy sleet;
No star illumines the heavy sky,
And darkness gathers at my feet.

When from a thorn-bush, dark and bare,
A small bird poured a sudden strain—
A slender note upon the air,
That pierced the stillness of my pain.

So frail a bird, so sweet a tone,
To challenge night’s encroaching shade!
He sang as if the dark alone
Were but the place where hope was made.

He knew no grief for ages past,
Nor cared what empires fall or rise;
He sang to match the icy blast,
And threw his joy against the skies.

And standing in the gather’d night,
I felt my weary spirit mend—
For in that song was secret light,
And life that lives beyond the end.
